result: HeLa metaphase spindles contain approximately 6300 MTs total, with 90-110 k-fibers comprising ~859 KMTs (approximately 9 KMTs per k-fiber), representing only ~14% of all spindle MTs.
evaluation: Claims C1, C14, C16, C17, and C18 are well-supported by quantitative electron tomography data from three complete spindle reconstructions (n=3 spindles, n=292 kinetochores). The measurements show consistent values across replicates with appropriate statistical reporting (mean ±STD), and the data are presented in multiple figures (Figure 2, Figure 3B) and tables (Table 1).

result: Only approximately half (49% ±15.5%) of KMT minus ends reach the spindle pole (defined as within 1.7 µm of the mother centriole), with an average of 4.1 ±2.0 KMTs per k-fiber at the pole compared to 8.5 ±2.2 at the kinetochore.
evaluation: Claims C2, C31, C32, and C33 are supported by systematic measurements of KMT minus-end positioning relative to a defined MT-centrosome interaction area (Figure 5C, Table 3). The definition of this interaction area is methodologically sound, based on the distribution of non-KMT minus ends. The conclusion of a semi-direct connection is appropriately inferred from the quantitative data.

result: K-fibers exhibit remarkable variation in circumference along their length, with polygonal cross-sectional areas approximately 3-4 fold larger at spindle poles (0.092 ±0.146 µm²) and spindle middle (0.149 ±0.210 µm²) compared to kinetochores (0.034 ±0.019 µm²), representing a broadening at the pole-proximal side.
evaluation: Claims C3, C4, and C44-C49 are supported by systematic cross-sectional analysis of k-fibers at 500 nm intervals along their length (Figure 7B, Table 4). The polygonal area measurements using the alpha shape algorithm are methodologically appropriate. Claim C52 synthesizes multiple measurements (tortuosity, density, area) and is well-supported by the combined data.

result: KMT minus-end associations with other MT lattices predominantly occur at spindle poles, with 60.7 ±9.4% of KMT-MT associations and 44.7 ±5.2% of KMT-non-KMT associations localized to pole regions at an interaction distance of 35 nm.
evaluation: Claims C5 and C53-C58 are supported by systematic analysis of MT-MT interactions at defined distances (Figure 8A-B, Tables 6-7). The choice of 35 nm as an example interaction distance is justified by reference to dynein motor dimensions. The normalization by local MT density is methodologically appropriate. The conclusion that poles are major sites of interaction is well-supported.

result: KMTs show a broad length distribution (average 3.87 ±1.98 µm) with ~20% shorter than 2 µm and ~39% longer than half-spindle length, while non-KMTs are shorter on average (2.0 ±1.7 µm) with an exponential distribution.
evaluation: Claims C28-C30 and C34 are supported by comprehensive length measurements of all traced MTs (n=2579 KMTs, n=14458 non-KMTs) across three spindles (Figure 4A-B, Table 3). The distributions are clearly different between KMTs and non-KMTs, supporting the conclusion that these MT populations have distinct properties.

result: KMTs display variable tortuosity (average 1.1 ±0.1) that correlates with length (R=0.68, p=2.2e-16) and position, with local tortuosity increasing from kinetochores toward spindle poles (R=-0.13, p=2.2e-16).
evaluation: Claims C36-C43 are supported by both global and local tortuosity measurements across all KMTs (n=2579) with appropriate statistical analysis (Figure 6E-I, Table 4). The correlation analyses include proper statistical tests with highly significant p-values. The segmentation approach (500 nm intervals) for local tortuosity is methodologically sound.

result: KMT density within k-fibers decreases at spindle poles, with only ~64% of KMTs enclosed in the defined k-fiber circle at poles compared to 100% at kinetochores.
evaluation: Claims C50 and C51 are supported by systematic density analysis along k-fiber length (Figure 7D, Table 4). The methodology of defining a circle at the kinetochore and tracking KMT inclusion along the fiber is appropriate. This result complements the cross-sectional area measurements.

result: The number of KMTs per k-fiber (average 8.5 ±2.2) is independent of both inter-kinetochore distance (Pearson's R=0.04 and 0.29) and k-fiber position within the spindle (central, intermediate, or peripheral).
evaluation: Claims C22, C23, and C83-C85 are supported by correlation analysis (Figure 3C-D) and positional analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 3N, Table 5). The lack of correlation is appropriately demonstrated with Pearson's coefficients near zero. The positional analysis includes adequate sample sizes across three regions.

result: At 35 nm interaction distance, 42 ±8% of KMT lattices associate with MT minus ends (predominantly non-KMT minus ends), with 59.8 ±6.7% of these associations occurring at spindle poles, while only 39.1 ±4.6% of non-KMT associations occur at poles.
evaluation: Claims C59-C63 are supported by reciprocal analysis of MT lattice-minus end associations (Figure 8C-D, Tables 8-9). The observation of a peak at relative position 0.3 for KMT-non-KMT associations (C63) is noted but requires cautious interpretation as it may reflect local MT density variations.

result: At 35 nm interaction distance, each KMT associates with 10.6 ±3.2 other MTs (average association length 145 ±186 nm), while non-KMTs associate with 7.4 ±3.1 other MTs (average length 103 ±118 nm), with KMTs showing higher numbers and lengths of associations at increasing distances.
evaluation: Claims C65 and C66 are supported by comprehensive MT-MT association analysis across multiple interaction distances (Tables 10-11, Figure 9—figure supplement 2). The trend of increasing associations with distance is consistent and well-documented. The large standard deviations reflect genuine biological variability in association patterns.

result: Kinetochores have an average area of 0.10 ±0.07 µm² with a KMT density of 112 ±60 KMTs/µm², corresponding to an average center-to-center KMT spacing of 74 ±22 nm (wall-to-wall spacing ~50 nm).
evaluation: Claims C24-C27 are supported by indirect measurements of kinetochore area and direct measurements of KMT spacing (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Tables 3-4). The calculation of wall-to-wall spacing from center-to-center distance is straightforward and appropriate. The indirect measurement approach is acknowledged as a limitation but is methodologically sound.

result: The reconstructed metaphase spindles had an average pole-to-pole distance of 9.0 ±1.7 µm and an average sister k-fiber distance of 1.13 ±0.24 µm.
evaluation: Claims C15 and C20 are supported by direct 3D measurements from the reconstructions (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Table 1). These measurements serve as validation that the spindles were captured at similar metaphase stages, supporting the comparative analysis across the three datasets.

result: Approximately 38 ±9% of non-KMT minus ends are localized in the MT-centrosome interaction zone, with the remaining ~60% in the spindle bulk.
evaluation: Claim C35 is supported by systematic analysis of non-KMT minus-end positioning (Figure 5E, Table 3). This measurement is important for defining the MT-centrosome interaction area and for comparison with KMT positioning.

result: The majority of KMTs display open flared ends at the kinetochore, consistent with previous observations in mammalian cells.
evaluation: Claim C19 is supported by electron microscopy images (Figure 2—figure supplement 4) and citation to previous work (McIntosh et al., 2013). This observation validates the identification of KMT plus ends and is consistent with established knowledge of KMT morphology.

result: The 3D reconstructions show a KMT length distribution in metaphase that is strikingly similar to distributions obtained by biophysical modeling combined with light microscopy in a parallel study.
evaluation: Claims C67 and C116 are supported by comparison with a parallel study (Conway et al., 2022). This cross-validation between electron microscopy and light microscopy/modeling strengthens confidence in both approaches. However, the evaluation is limited to the discussion section and relies on external data.

result: KMTs are on average twice as long as non-KMTs (3.87 µm vs 2.0 µm), contributing to a higher percentage of tubulin mass in KMTs (~25%) compared to their numerical representation (~14%).
evaluation: Claims C68 and C69 are supported by the length distribution data (Figure 4, Table 3) and cross-referenced with light microscopy measurements from the parallel study. The inference about tubulin mass is logical and supported by the length difference, though the 25% tubulin mass value comes from the parallel study rather than direct measurement here.

result: KMT length distributions in HeLa cells show striking similarities to C. elegans, with both showing flat distributions and low numbers of very short/long KMTs, while non-KMTs in both systems show exponential distributions typical of dynamic instability, indicating KMTs have distinct properties including possibly higher stability.
evaluation: Claims C70-C75 are supported by comparison of the current data with previous work on C. elegans (Redemann et al., 2017) and citations to studies on MT dynamics (Burbank et al., 2007; Loiodice et al., 2019). The inference about KMT stability (C74) is appropriately qualified as speculative but is well-supported by the length distribution differences.

result: K-fibers in HeLa cells mediate a semi-direct connection with spindle poles, where at least one KMT directly contacts the pole while others are indirectly linked via non-KMTs, similar to the pattern observed in C. elegans.
evaluation: Claims C93 and C94 synthesize multiple lines of evidence (KMT length distribution, minus-end positioning, MT-MT associations) and are supported by citations to previous work (McDonald et al., 1992; O'Toole et al., 2020). This is a major interpretive conclusion that is well-supported by the data, though alternative interpretations are acknowledged (C98).

result: Centrally located KMTs are shorter with minus ends closer to the mother centriole compared to peripheral KMTs, likely related to spindle roundedness.
evaluation: Claims C95 and C96 are supported by positional analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 4, Table 5). The interpretation relating this to spindle roundedness (C96) is speculative but reasonable, supported by citation to previous work (Taubenberger et al., 2020). This represents a secondary observation that adds nuance to the main findings.

result: KMTs and non-KMTs show correlations in number and length of associations, but differ in spatial patterns: KMTs preferentially associate at spindle poles (independent of interaction distance), while non-KMTs show flat patterns at 25-35 nm and increased central associations at 35-50 nm.
evaluation: Claims C101-C106 are supported by comprehensive spatial analysis of MT-MT associations (Figures 8F-G, 9C-D, Figure 8—figure supplement 1F). The interpretation regarding interpolar MTs (C106) is supported by citations to previous studies (Kajtez et al., 2016; Mastronarde et al., 1993; Vukušić et al., 2017).

result: The difference in KMT number between HeLa (~9 KMTs) and PtK1 cells (~20 KMTs) could be related to kinetochore size, with HeLa kinetochores (~0.107 µm²) being approximately half the size of PtK1 kinetochores (~0.157 µm²), potentially defining available MT binding sites.
evaluation: Claims C78-C82 are speculative comparisons with previous work. While the size measurements are supported by data (C81 from current study, C79-C80 from citations), the causal relationship (C78, C82) is not directly tested. The correlation between kinetochore size and KMT number is plausible but requires experimental validation. This represents reasonable speculation rather than demonstrated fact.

result: Increased KMT tortuosity at spindle poles might promote anchoring of broadened k-fibers into the non-KMT network through MT-MT interactions.
evaluation: Claim C97 is speculative, proposing a mechanistic explanation for the observed structural features. While the increased tortuosity and broadening are well-documented, the proposed functional consequence (promoting anchoring) is not directly tested. This represents a reasonable hypothesis for future investigation.

result: A model is proposed where KMTs nucleate at kinetochores and grow toward poles along trajectories defined by well-aligned non-KMTs, with spindles behaving as active liquid crystals showing high nematic order near chromosomes (S=0.81±0.02) and lower order at poles (S=0.54±0.02), potentially explaining k-fiber broadening at poles.
evaluation: Claims C107-C113 synthesize findings from the current study with a parallel study (Conway et al., 2022) and theoretical frameworks (Brugués and Needleman, 2014; Oriola et al., 2020). The nematic order parameters (C110-C111) come from the parallel study. The integration is logical and well-supported, though C113 is appropriately qualified as speculative. This represents an important interpretive framework.

result: Plastic sections undergo collapse in the electron beam during imaging, but this Z-dimension loss can be corrected by expanding the complete stack of serial tomograms, which was done for all three datasets.
evaluation: Claims C114 and C115 address a critical methodological issue. The sample collapse is well-documented in the literature (citations provided), and the correction method is clearly described (Figure 2—figure supplement 2). The Z-factors applied (1.3-1.42) are reasonable. This methodological correction is essential for accurate measurements.

result: Light and electron microscopy produce truly complementary data, despite requiring completely different sample preparation and data analysis methods.
evaluation: Claim C117 is supported by the comparison with the parallel study (Conway et al., 2022) showing agreement in KMT length distributions. This represents an important validation of both approaches and demonstrates the value of multi-modal imaging.

result: Background knowledge claims about mitotic spindles, KMT organization across species, and previous measurements in other cell types are accurately cited and contextualized.
evaluation: Claims C6-C13 represent accurate citations to established literature and provide appropriate context for the current study. These are well-supported by the cited references and represent accurate knowledge claims.

result: Cold-treated cells show cold-stable k-fibers while non-KMTs depolymerize, with KMTs likely stabilized by kinetochore interactions and/or KMT-KMT/KMT-non-KMT associations mediated by MT-associated proteins.
evaluation: Claims C76 and C77 are supported by citation to previous work (Maiato et al., 2004) and additional citations for proposed mechanisms (Brinkley and Cartwright, 1975; DeLuca et al., 2006; Warren et al., 2020; Agarwal, 2018). The mechanistic explanation (C77) is appropriately qualified as speculative.

result: KMTs in reconstructed k-fibers are of different lengths (confirming previous observations), with ~20% shorter than 2 µm and half of KMT minus ends not positioned in the MT-centrosome interaction area, though only 5% of k-fibers have no KMTs reaching the pole.
evaluation: Claims C86-C90 are supported by the length distribution data (Figure 4A) and minus-end positioning analysis (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 3). These observations are important for understanding k-fiber organization and are consistent with previous studies (citations provided).

result: In C. elegans one-cell embryos, only ~20% of KMT minus ends were within 2 µm of the mother centriole, suggesting the majority of KMTs do not contact centrosomes.
evaluation: Claims C91 and C92 refer to previous work by the authors on C. elegans. These are appropriately cited and provide important comparative context for interpreting the HeLa cell data.

result: The results do not exclude alternative models where k-fibers are tight bundles with changing MT composition along their length, with differences in KMT length potentially reflecting MT exchange with the spindle, consistent with dynamic k-fiber maturation in metaphase.
evaluation: Claims C98-C100 appropriately acknowledge alternative interpretations of the data. This represents good scientific practice in recognizing that the static EM snapshots cannot definitively distinguish between different dynamic models. The acknowledgment is supported by citations to relevant work (Begley et al., 2021; Maiato et al., 2004).
